intro: Janáček’s lament for a carpenter killed during the Brno university demonstrations begins with a broken piano phrase. It comes back again and again, gathering chords around it until the opening whisper becomes a cry.

sections.label: A · A phrase after a rest
sections.mNote: A small upward leap, then a fall back

sections.label: A · The opening played again
sections.mNote: The repeat brings back the quiet E♭-minor phrase

cues.title: A rest before the phrase
cues.text: Each little phrase begins after a rest. The right hand leaps from B♭ to E♭ and falls back; the left hand moves beneath it, then both settle on a held chord. Janáček marks the movement Adagio, with the quaver moving at 56.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, plate H.M. 339, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 9, opening of Smrt. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/62/IMSLP57304-PMLP117865-Jan%C3%A1%C4%8Dek_-_1.X.1905_%28%27Sonata%27%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A carpenter in Brno
cues.text: In October 1905 Brno’s streets fill with rival demonstrations over a proposed Czech university. Troops are called in. The carpenter František Pavlík is fatally wounded; on 2 October, the day he dies, Janáček begins this sonata.
cues.evidence: Leoš Janáček Foundation, work history and chronology for 1. X. 1905. https://janacek-nadace.cz/dilo-leose-janacka/dila/1-x-1905/

cues.title: The phrase starts again
cues.text: The first paragraph is repeated. The same small leap, the same pauses, the same brief flare of forte disturb its quiet. At the end of the repeat, a different ending takes the piano into new chords.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 9: opening repeat with first and second endings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The pianist saves a copy
cues.text: At a rehearsal on the day of the 1906 première, Janáček burns the sonata’s third movement. Later he throws the remaining manuscript into the Vltava. The pianist Ludmila Tučková keeps her copy of the first two movements; in 1924 she brings it forward, and they reach print.
cues.evidence: Leoš Janáček Foundation, work history: destruction of the finale, loss of the manuscript and Tučková’s surviving copy. https://janacek-nadace.cz/dilo-leose-janacka/dila/1-x-1905/

cues.title: Quick answers below
cues.text: The melody keeps its clipped phrases, while the left hand grows restless. Quick figures answer beneath it and spread into repeated chords. Crescendos push the piano from piano through forte to fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), pp. 9–10, continuation after the second ending and successive written crescendos.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The left hand persists
cues.text: The left hand’s rapid chords now continue through the right hand’s rests. Above them, the melody is pared down to accented fragments, sometimes only two notes. The piano has lost the breathing room of the opening.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), pp. 10–11: continuous left-hand figures beneath rests and accented melodic fragments.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The whisper becomes a cry
cues.text: The opening phrase returns in E♭ minor, marked sforzando fortissimo. Its small leap is unchanged. Underneath it the left hand keeps moving, filling the gaps that once left the melody exposed.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12, a tempo return marked sff, with continued left-hand chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last soft chord
cues.text: The returning phrases become quiet again. The last line reaches pianississimo; for the final E♭-minor chord Janáček asks for una corda, the piano’s soft pedal. The bass E♭ lies far below the closely packed notes above.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12, final two systems: ppp, una corda and final E♭-minor chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Back to the first rest
transitions.from: A · A phrase after a rest
transitions.how: The first ending dwindles to a held chord under the soft pedal. The repeat then restores the opening E♭-minor bass and the right hand’s small upward leap. The little rest before the phrase returns too.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 9: first ending, una corda, repeat sign and opening phrase.

transitions.title: The second ending continues
transitions.to: Dev · Chords under the broken phrase
transitions.how: The second ending carries the piano past the repeat. Held bass notes support the clipped melody, then the left hand starts answering with quick chord figures of its own. The phrases still begin after rests, but the accompaniment increasingly fills the spaces between them.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), pp. 9–10: second ending and the development of rapid left-hand figures.

transitions.title: The opening returns with force
transitions.from: Dev · The left hand keeps moving
transitions.how: A ritenuto checks the rapid left-hand chords. At a tempo the opening melody returns over an E♭-minor bass, marked sff. The left hand carries on with moving chords, so the familiar phrase arrives amid the motion built up in the middle.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12: ritenuto followed by the a tempo return.

transitions.title: The phrases dwindle
transitions.to: Coda · Last phrases and soft pedal
transitions.how: The right hand repeats the short falling phrases while the left hand continues its quieter chords. Janáček brings the final line down to ppp, then writes una corda over the last E♭-minor chord. A low E♭ anchors the close.
transitions.evidence: Hudební matice score, Štědroň reissue (1949), p. 12, closing systems.

composer.epithet: He wrote down the voices of strangers in Brno, then gave opera some of its most painfully recognisable people.
facts: Chorister in Old Brno; organ studies in Prague; conservatories in Leipzig and Vienna
Founded the Organ School in 1881; directed it until 1919
Nine operas, two string quartets, Sinfonietta, Glagolitic Mass, piano music and folk-song collections
composer.background:
In August 1865, Janáček’s mother took her eleven-year-old son to Brno and left him at the Augustinian monastery. His father, a schoolmaster in Hukvaldy, was ill; the family needed the scholarship. Nearly sixty years later, in his autobiographical sketch of 1924, Janáček remembered “a hard bed, harder bread. No caresses.” The monastery’s choirmaster, Pavel Křížkovský, taught him music. The boy sang at services, went to concerts and the theatre, and learned the profession that would keep him in Brno for the rest of his life.

He trained as a teacher, studied at the Prague Organ School, and tried the conservatories in Leipzig and Vienna. Prague also gave him a lasting friendship with Dvořák. Back in Brno he taught, conducted the Beseda choir and organised concerts; in 1881 he founded the Organ School, which he directed until 1919. His programmes included Beethoven’s Missa solemnis and Dvořák’s Stabat mater. The composer who would eventually make an orchestra speak in sharp, unfinished sentences spent much of his working life rehearsing other men’s long ones.
